sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

In this lesson you'll have a real conversation with a local model, understand how model sizes affect speed and quality, and see how Ollama's API works — the same API that Continue.dev and Claude Code will use in the next two lessons.

## Running a Model Interactively

Once a model is downloaded, running it is a single command:

```
ollama run phi4
```

This starts an interactive session. You type your message, press Enter, and the model responds — all on your machine.

To exit the session, type `/bye` and press Enter.

Some useful commands inside an Ollama session:
```
/help        — list all session commands
/clear       — clear conversation history
/show info   — show the current model's details
/bye         — exit
```

## Understanding Model Sizes

Models are described by their parameter count: 3B, 7B, 13B, 70B. The number refers to billions of parameters — the learned numerical weights that make up the model's "knowledge."

Here's the practical guide:

| Size | RAM Needed | Speed | Quality | Best For |
|------|-----------|-------|---------|----------|
| 3B | ~4GB | Very fast | Basic | Simple Q&A, short summaries, fast completion |
| 7B | ~8GB | Fast | Good | Most everyday tasks, code explanation, drafting |
| 13B | ~16GB | Moderate | Better | Reasoning, longer documents, more nuanced output |
| 70B | ~64GB | Slow (CPU) | Excellent | Near-frontier quality (needs dedicated GPU for speed) |

For most people, the 7B tier is the practical sweet spot: capable enough for real work, fast enough to feel responsive, and manageable in RAM.

**Quantization:** You'll see model tags like `:q4_K_M` or `:fp16`. These indicate how the model weights are compressed. Q4 quantization (4-bit) makes models about 4× smaller with minimal quality loss — most Ollama models use this by default, which is why the file sizes are smaller than you'd expect.

**Why does "3B" mean 3 billion?** Each parameter is a number that the model learned during training. GPT-3 had 175B parameters. Claude and GPT-4 are estimated at hundreds of billions to trillions. A 3B local model is genuinely small by comparison — but modern training techniques mean small models punch above their weight for focused tasks.

## The Ollama Model Library

Ollama hosts a curated library at `ollama.com/library`. The major model families you'll encounter:

**Llama (Meta)** — The most widely used family. `llama3.2:3b` is great for fast tasks. `llama3.3:70b` rivals frontier models but needs serious hardware.

**Phi (Microsoft)** — Microsoft's compact models punch above their weight for code and reasoning. `phi4` is excellent for 9GB. `phi3.5:mini` is smaller and very fast.

**Mistral / Mixtral** — French AI lab known for strong coding ability. `mistral:7b` is a reliable workhorse.

**Gemma (Google)** — Google's open model family. `gemma2:9b` has strong instruction-following.

**Qwen (Alibaba)** — Strong multilingual models, particularly good for Chinese text. `qwen2.5:7b` is a solid choice.

**DeepSeek-R1** — Strong reasoning model from a Chinese lab. Good for math and code at small sizes.

Pull any of these with `ollama pull <name>`.

## Using the API Directly

Ollama's API at `localhost:11434` works even when you're not in an interactive session. Here's how to call it from PowerShell:

```
$body = @{
    model = "phi4"
    prompt = "What is the capital of France? One word answer."
    stream = $false
} | ConvertTo-Json

Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "http://localhost:11434/api/generate" `
    -Method POST `
    -ContentType "application/json" `
    -Body $body
```

You'll see a JSON response with a `response` field containing the model's answer.

The API also supports the OpenAI chat format at `/v1/chat/completions` — which is exactly what Connect.dev, Claude Code, and other tools use to connect.

**Speed tip:** The first response after loading a model is slow — the model has to load into RAM ("warm up"). Subsequent responses in the same session are much faster because the model stays loaded. If you're doing repeated tasks, keep the session open instead of relaunching.

sections.title: Run a Model and Compare to Claude
sections.content:
You need at least one model downloaded from lesson 12-2. Use `phi4` or `llama3.2:3b` depending on what you pulled.

**Step 1 — Pull a second model (if you only have one):**
If you pulled `phi4`, also get the small Llama:
```
ollama pull llama3.2:3b
```
If you pulled `llama3.2:3b`, get Phi-4 (if you have the disk space):
```
ollama pull phi4
```

**Step 2 — Ask both models the same question:**

Run this prompt in each model:
```
ollama run phi4 "Explain recursion in programming using a real-world analogy. Be concise."
```
Then:
```
ollama run llama3.2:3b "Explain recursion in programming using a real-world analogy. Be concise."
```

**Observe:** Which was faster? Which gave a better explanation?

**Step 3 — Ask a coding question:**
```
ollama run phi4 "Write a JavaScript function that takes an array of numbers and returns only the even ones."
```
Run the same prompt on your other model. Compare the code quality.

**Step 4 — Test it on a private task:**
Type something you would NOT want to send to a cloud service — maybe summarizing a personal note, reviewing a private document, or asking a question you'd prefer to keep private. See how well the local model handles it.

**Step 5 — Compare to Claude:**
Open Claude.ai and ask the same recursion question. Write two observations:
- What did the local model do better or worse?
- Was the quality difference enough to matter for this specific task?

**Save your notes.** In lesson 12-7 you'll build a full model selection guide based on observations like these.

sections.title: Workshop A — Model Speed Benchmarking
sections.content:
Measure the performance of your local models.

**Step 1 — Run a speed test** for each model you have installed:
```powershell
# Time a response
$start = Get-Date
ollama run phi3:mini "Write a 200-word story about a robot learning to paint" --nowordwrap
$elapsed = (Get-Date) - $start
Write-Host "Time: $($elapsed.TotalSeconds) seconds"
```

**Step 2 — Record metrics for each model:**
| Model | Load time | Tokens/sec | RAM usage | Quality |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| phi3:mini | | | | |
| qwen2.5-coder:7b | | | | |

**Step 3 — Monitor RAM usage** while a model is running:
```powershell
Get-Process ollama | Select-Object CPU, WorkingSet64
```

**Step 4 — Find your "sweet spot"** — the model with the best quality/speed trade-off for your hardware.

**Step 5 — Ask Claude:** "At my speed of [X tokens/sec], how does local model speed compare to typing speed, reading speed, and cloud API speed?"

sections.title: Workshop B — Build a Real Task with a Local Model
sections.content:
Complete a real-world task using only your local model.

**Step 1 — Choose a task** that you'd normally use cloud AI for but that involves sensitive content:
- Review proprietary code for issues
- Draft a confidential document
- Analyse sensitive business data

**Step 2 — Complete the task entirely locally.** Do not send any data to cloud AI.

**Step 3 — Evaluate the output quality.** On a scale of 1-10 compared to Claude Sonnet:
- Was the output correct?
- Was it detailed enough?
- Did it understand your intent?

**Step 4 — Identify quality gaps.** What would have been better with a cloud model?

**Step 5 — Mandatory review:** Ask your local model: *"Review your own output above. What are the weaknesses or errors in your response?"* Compare its self-assessment to your own evaluation.

sections.title: Workshop C — Model Cards and Capability Research
sections.content:
Learn to research local model capabilities before downloading.

**Step 1 — Visit ollama.com/library** and look up the model cards for 3 models you're interested in.

**Step 2 — For each model, find:**
- Context window size (how much text it can process at once)
- Training focus (general vs code vs chat)
- Benchmark scores (MMLU, HumanEval, etc. if listed)
- Model family and who created it

**Step 3 — Ask Claude:** *"Explain these benchmark scores: MMLU, HumanEval, GSM8K, GPQA. What does each test and what score would indicate a model is suitable for general coding tasks?"*

**Step 4 — Compare benchmark scores** for your installed models vs Claude Haiku and Sonnet (look these up from Anthropic's model card).

**Step 5 — Develop intuition:** For your typical coding tasks, what benchmark score would be "good enough"?

sections.title: Workshop D — Custom Model Configuration
sections.content:
Create custom Ollama modelfiles for your specific use cases.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude:** "What is an Ollama Modelfile? How can I use it to customise a model's system prompt, temperature, and context window?"

**Step 2 — Create a custom modelfile** for your code review use case:
```dockerfile
FROM qwen2.5-coder:7b

PARAMETER temperature 0.1
PARAMETER num_ctx 8192

SYSTEM """
You are an expert code reviewer. Your role is to:
1. Find bugs and logic errors
2. Identify security issues
3. Suggest performance improvements
4. Check for adherence to SOLID principles

Be specific about line numbers and exact issues. Prioritise critical issues.
"""
```

**Step 3 — Create the model:**
```powershell
ollama create code-reviewer -f ./Modelfile
```

**Step 4 — Test the custom model** on real code. Does the system prompt improve its code review quality?

**Step 5 — Create a second custom model** for another use case (documentation writer, test generator, etc.).

sections.question: You run a local model and it keeps losing context from earlier in a long conversation. What is most likely happening?
options: The model has a memory bug
The conversation has exceeded the model's context window — earlier messages are being truncated to fit within the limit
Ollama is not storing conversation history
You need to restart Ollama to refresh the context
sections.explanation: Every model has a maximum context window (e.g., 4096, 8192, or 128000 tokens). When a conversation exceeds this limit, older messages are dropped. Local models often have smaller context windows than cloud models. Solutions: (1) use a model with a larger context window, (2) configure `num_ctx` in the Modelfile to use more context (at the cost of more RAM), (3) periodically summarise and restart with a compressed history.

sections.question: A local model produces high-quality responses but takes 45 seconds per response. This is acceptable for which use case?
options: Real-time code completion as you type
Overnight batch processing of 100 documents where speed doesn't matter
All use cases — quality is worth the wait
sections.explanation: 45 seconds per response is too slow for any interactive use case where users expect near-real-time feedback. Batch processing is the right use case: if you're generating summaries or analyses overnight, response time doesn't matter as long as the quality is good. For interactive use, either use a smaller/faster local model (accepting quality trade-off) or switch to cloud AI for interactive tasks while keeping local for privacy-sensitive batch work.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 12-3.** You've run local models interactively and have a first-hand sense of the quality/speed tradeoffs. Next: LM Studio, the GUI interface for the same models.
